entries.title: How Cozey turns its operators into software builders on Vercel

entries.content:
• Employees outside engineering, including warehouse, finance, and support staff, are now building applications and deploying them to Vercel

  • Finance uses an app it built to review profit and loss weekly instead of monthly

  • Adopting Vercel Flags allowed Cozey to retire a separate tool that cost approximately $80,000 annually

  • Six projects, including the storefront, use AI Gateway

Cozey is a Canadian furniture company that makes modular sofas customers can configure for their homes. It runs its storefront and most of its back-office applications on Vercel. Warehouse, finance, and customer support employees now securely deploy their own apps on that same platform.

Copy link to headingTurning everyday problems into working applications

CEO Fred Aubé encourages employees to solve problems they encounter without waiting for another team to take them on. Sam Morrison, VP of Digital, saw teams reach the limits of what they could prototype in an AI chat. Employees used coding agents to build web apps. With Vercel, they could deploy an app themselves and give coworkers a link to a working tool.

In the warehouse, a coordinator built a live floor plan that shows where boxes sit and what staff are doing. Sam says engineering would not have prioritized that project. Finance built its own app to track profit and loss and now uses it to review performance every week instead of once a month.

A customer support representative built an app that uses AI to generate images of Cozey furniture in a customer’s own room. In October, Cozey planned to make the tool available to shoppers.

Sam says a new app appears almost every week.

Every problem they solve for themselves is a problem I don’t need to deal with. And if they come up with something really cool, I get to steal it and integrate it into what we’re doing.Sam MorrisonVP of Digital @ Cozey

Copy link to headingExtending Vercel from the storefront to the business behind it

Sam estimates that the Atmosphere sofa collection alone has about 1.2 million possible configurations. Cozey worked with an agency specializing in Next.js to rebuild its storefront on Vercel. With a custom front end, the team could decide how shoppers explore those options.

We want the most control possible. We could do a Shopify template, or we could build our own front end on Next.js that we have total control over. We’re gonna go that way 100% of the time.Sam MorrisonVP of Digital @ Cozey

Cozey uses Fluid compute for functions on the storefront. It runs internal Python backends and the Cozey Operating System, or C.O.S., on Vercel. Teams use C.O.S. to forecast orders, manage warehouse and retail operations, review finances, and track business performance. Operating margin depends in part on how quickly furniture moves from incoming containers to customer shipments.

Each C.O.S. pull request gets a Vercel Preview Deployment, giving the team a working application to test before release. Cozey’s engineers reported that with caching, builds on Vercel took a couple of minutes. They also share preview links with Fred so he can try changes and give feedback.

The team uses Vercel Flags to control how new features reach users, replacing a separate tool that cost approximately $80,000 annually. After release, performance metrics on Vercel give the team a common reference for checking how applications are running.

When Cozey launched in Australia, the team had regional backend work to do. For the storefront on Vercel, Sam says, “it wasn’t even a conversation.”

Copy link to headingManaging access as more people build

As more employees began building, Cozey needed to manage who could open their applications and who could deploy and maintain them. An employee once deployed an app that anyone on the internet could open. For internal apps that had shipped without appropriate authentication, Sam turned on access protection on Vercel.

“It saved us from some pretty serious privacy risks,” says Sam.

Cozey uses single sign-on so members of its Vercel team can sign in with company credentials. The company manages team membership through groups in its employee directory with Directory Sync.

Copy link to headingGiving AI applications a common way to access models

As more teams built with AI, Sam saw them repeating the work of connecting to models. Six Cozey projects, including the storefront, send model requests through Vercel AI Gateway. Cozey’s engineers use it to call models from their code editors, too. Sam wants all of Cozey’s model requests to go through Gateway.

AI Gateway gives teams one interface for different model providers. If a provider is unavailable, the gateway can route the request to another provider that serves the same model. It adds no markup to provider token prices. Sam describes the added cost of routing requests through it as “basically $0 in additional overhead.”

The company is also developing what it calls the Agentic Mesh, a system to coordinate AI use across internal applications and customer experiences. The coordinating service is being built on AWS, with AI Gateway planned for model requests and Vercel for application deployment. It is intended to help teams decide which models to use and where to run applications, while giving engineering visibility into AI usage and costs.

The mesh is our single control plane. I want control, observability, governance, all of those fundamental pieces in place, so that when we enter this future, we’re doing it in the safest, most secure, most private way possible.Sam MorrisonVP of Digital @ Cozey

Copy link to headingWhat's next

Sam says engineering wouldn’t have prioritized a live map of the warehouse floor. The coordinator who needed to see where the boxes were could make a different call, build the map, and share it with the people moving them. When the digital team sees an idea worth taking further, it has a working app to build on.

Cozey chose a custom storefront on Vercel so it could decide how shoppers explore its furniture. Sam’s next goal is for employees outside engineering to share that control. If shoppers keep asking the same question about a sofa, the support rep who hears it could put the answer on the product page.

entries.content:
All Vercel Sandbox runtimes now use Vercel Managed Images (VMIs).

Legacy runtimes, such as 

node22
, now use the open-source images in the vercel/sandbox repository, distributed through Vercel Container Registry (VCR). Sandboxes created with these now come with 64 GB of storage and use the same infrastructure as sandboxes powered by VCR.

The universal image is released nightly, and rolling tags such as 

latest
pick up operating system, dependency, and coding agent updates. Pin an image digest when you need a reproducible environment.

Sandboxes created with version 3 or later of the JavaScript Sandbox SDK use 

vercel/sandbox/universal:latest
by default. The universal image includes Node.js, Python, coding agents such as Claude Code and Pi, and common utilities. You can pull it at 
vcr.vercel.com/vercel/sandbox/universal:latest
.

Learn more in the Sandbox documentation.

entries.title: AWS PrivateLink endpoints are now available on Secure Compute
entries.summary: Enterprise teams using Secure Compute can now create and manage AWS PrivateLink endpoints directly from the Vercel dashboard.Endpoints on Secure Compute live in your team's dedicated VPC and use the network's AWS region. They belong to the network and are shared by its connected project environments.Vercel Functions, Vercel Sandbox, and builds connected to the network can reach AWS-hosted backends
entries.content:
Enterprise teams using Secure Compute can now create and manage AWS PrivateLink endpoints directly from the Vercel dashboard.

Endpoints on Secure Compute live in your team's dedicated VPC and use the network's AWS region. They belong to the network and are shared by its connected project environments.

Vercel Functions, Vercel Sandbox, and builds connected to the network can reach AWS-hosted backends over the AWS private network. Before you add an endpoint in Vercel, the backend must already be exposed through a published AWS PrivateLink endpoint service. Examples include RDS, Aurora, Redshift, Snowflake, MongoDB Atlas, and internal services behind a Network Load Balancer.

In Team Settings → Networking, open your Secure Compute network and choose Add Endpoint from the PrivateLink tab.

Standard pricing for new endpoints:

  • Each Secure Compute network includes one AWS PrivateLink endpoint. Additional endpoints cost $30 per month each.

  • PrivateLink data transfer costs $0.04 per GB.

Read the Secure Compute PrivateLink documentation to get started.

entries.content:
With 

flags@4.5.0
, projects on Vercel can use Flags Explorer and precompute without 

FLAGS_SECRET
. That cuts out a setup step for new projects and removes the need to keep a shared secret in sync across microfrontends.

Vercel signs Flags Explorer discovery requests and overrides, and the SDK encrypts flag values shown in the Vercel Toolbar with Vercel’s public key.

Existing projects keep using 

FLAGS_SECRET
while the environment variable is set or the secret is passed in code. Upgrading alone doesn't switch them to Vercel-managed keys. To use Vercel-managed keys for these features, remove the environment variable and any code that passes the secret explicitly. For local development, run 
vercel env pull
.

Precomputed codes created without a secret work only in the deployment that created them. Precompute without a secret requires Vercel system environment variables, which are enabled by default. Prebuilt deployments and codes that must work across deployments still need a secret; use 

FLAGS_PRECOMPUTE_SECRET
if only precompute needs one. If you use a build cache, see the precompute documentation for the required configuration.

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

Ask it in plain language to:Manage virtual models: Create reusable model IDs with saved settings, then list, inspect, update, or restore them.Configure routing rules: View, add, and update team-wide rules that redirect requests to another model or block them.Set spending budgets: View and set budgets for your team, projects, and members, and
entries.content:
Your agent can now manage AI Gateway through Vercel MCP. Ask it in plain language to:

  • Manage virtual models: Create reusable model IDs with saved settings, then list, inspect, update, or restore them.

  • Configure routing rules: View, add, and update team-wide rules that redirect requests to another model or block them.

  • Set spending budgets: View and set budgets for your team, projects, and members, and configure defaults.

To create a virtual model, for example, ask your agent:

Create a virtual model named coding-agent that uses anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 with Zero Data Retention enabled.

Your apps and coding agents using AI Gateway can then use 

vmc/coding-agent
as the model ID. You can change its model or settings later without updating those clients or redeploying your app.

To get started, connect your agent to Vercel MCP with team-level access and the required AI Gateway permissions. Your Vercel team permissions still apply.

entries.summary: The Workflow SDK now lets you delete a finished run's stored data on demand. This feature gives you the ability to quickly meet compliance and security requirements when sensitive data needs to be purged from run payloads.Deleting a run's data deletes any inputs, outputs, hook payloads, and error traces for the run and its related entities. This does not delete the run's metadata: the run is still
entries.content:
The Workflow SDK now lets you delete a finished run's stored data on demand. This feature gives you the ability to quickly meet compliance and security requirements when sensitive data needs to be purged from run payloads.

Deleting a run's data deletes any inputs, outputs, hook payloads, and error traces for the run and its related entities. This does not delete the run's metadata: the run is still listed in observability. Attributes, hook tokens, and timings for steps and events can still be inspected.

You can delete a run's data from the Vercel Dashboard, or via the CLI:

      
# Locallypnpx workflow delete # For runs on Vercelpnpx workflow delete  --backend vercel --env preview

You can also delete a run's data programmatically from your code:

      
import { deleteRuns, getRun } from 'workflow/api';
await getRun(runId).delete();       // one runawait deleteRuns([runIdA, runIdB]); // up to 100 runs

Deletion applies to finished runs only, so a run that is still going is skipped and keeps running. If you want to delete a run's payload as soon as it finishes, use the retention settings instead.

Upgrade to 

workflow@5.7.0
or higher to use this feature. Learn more in the 
deleteRuns()
reference.

entries.content:
Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines is now available on AI Gateway. The small multimodal reasoning model is built for agentic coding, tool use, and knowledge work, with text and image inputs and text output.

Inkling 2 Mini has 26.4 billion total parameters and 3.4 billion active per token. The model runs its middle layers more than once for every token, which lets it reason further before writing anything down and often reach an answer with fewer reasoning tokens. Like Inkling 2 Small, it is strongest on long-running agentic tasks.

The model has a 1M-token context window, and reasoning effort can be set from 

none
through 
max
.

Use 

thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini
as the model name: 
      
import { streamText } from 'ai';
const result = streamText({  model: 'thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini',  prompt: 'Write a Python script that renames photos by the date they were taken.',});
for await (const text of result.textStream) {  process.stdout.write(text);}

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

      
npx vercel ai-gateway setup

Then select 

thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini
in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Inkling 2 Mini in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

entries.title: AI Gateway now runs canary ZDR audits
entries.summary: AI Gateway now runs canary audits against inference providers to detect when prompt content is read outside the inference path.Contractual Zero Data Retention (ZDR) agreements and point-in-time security audits establish how a provider should handle your data, but production infrastructure changes continuously. Canary audits add a detection layer on top.Each canary audit run:Mints unique URLs that
entries.content:
AI Gateway now runs canary audits against inference providers to detect when prompt content is read outside the inference path.

Contractual Zero Data Retention (ZDR) agreements and point-in-time security audits establish how a provider should handle your data, but production infrastructure changes continuously. Canary audits add a detection layer on top.

Each canary audit run:

  1. Mints unique URLs that exist nowhere else, each mapped privately to a specific provider, model, and audit run.

  2. Sends prompts containing those URLs through the normal inference path, with ZDR requested for covered providers and non-ZDR pairs included as positive controls.

  3. Watches for traffic. A ZDR provider should never retain, inspect, or crawl prompt content, so a canary URL should never receive a request.

  4. Records any request to a canary URL, identifying the provider, model, and run for investigation.

Canary audits complement contractual ZDR agreements and independent audits rather than replacing them.

Read more about AI Gateway security and compliance measures in the documentation.

entries.content:
日本語版はこちら：Vercel日本法人の代表に花尾和成が就任いたしました

Kazunari Hanao has joined Vercel as Country Manager for Japan, based in Tokyo. His appointment is part of our continued investment in the Japanese market, including plans to expand our local team.

Japanese developers were early adopters of Next.js. And today, Vercel's customers in Japan include Mitsubishi Corporation, Fujitsu Limited, U-NEXT CO., Ltd., and DeNA Co., Ltd., alongside startups like SANU Inc. and Reiwa Travel, Inc.

Kazunari has spent the last decade building and leading software businesses in Japan. He joins Vercel from Pendo, where he was President of Pendo Japan. Before that, he built HashiCorp’s Japan business and spent nearly five years in sales leadership at Pivotal in Tokyo.

I asked him about the opportunity in Japan and his decision to join Vercel.

Copy link to headingWhy are you optimistic about Vercel's future in Japan?

Japan is at a turning point in how software gets built. The country has innovative companies and talented developers, but complex enterprise IT environments are slowing the adoption of frontier AI to the point that businesses can’t capture its value.

Vercel’s opportunity is to help Japanese enterprises move from experimentation to production, and run AI applications securely, reliably, and efficiently at scale. Cost, governance, and security for AI have become business priorities, not just technical ones. Almost every CXO I've met recently is working through those questions.

Copy link to headingWhat interested you in working for Vercel?

I've always been drawn to technology that simplifies complexity and helps businesses move faster. Vercel felt like a natural continuation of that, with bigger potential. AI is transforming the whole software development lifecycle, and Vercel has a real chance to become a foundational platform for the next generation of applications.

Ultimately what convinced me was the vision, the developer-first culture, and the chance to build something in Japan from the ground up. I enjoy building businesses, bringing talented people together, and creating an environment where teams feel empowered to take on hard problems. Vercel gives me the chance to do that with technology I believe in.

Copy link to headingWhat have you learned building businesses in Japan for global companies?

Building a successful business is about much more than growing revenue. It starts with bringing together the right people, uniting them around a shared goal, earning the trust of customers and partners, and building a culture where every team member feels ownership.

I've also learned how much it matters to connect global innovation with the specific needs of Japanese customers. During our first meetings, Guillermo and I talked about a future where countless digital services in Japan run on Vercel, and people experience its value every day whether they realize it or not. "Vercel Everywhere" is the future I want to build.

Copy link to headingWhat’s next in 2027

We're bringing our flagship conference, Ship, to Tokyo for the first time in 2027. It's a chance to hear directly from the Vercel team and from Japanese companies building on the platform. We'll share more details at vercel.com/ship in the new year.

We’re also growing our Tokyo team across sales, solutions engineering, and partnerships. A larger local team will help us support Japanese customers and deepen our partnerships with Classmethod, AWS Japan, and Sitecore Japan. Watch our careers page for upcoming opportunities in Japan.
